summary: Hard-fighting member of the cod family caught from wharves, breakwaters, and boats throughout the Maritimes, with the Bay of Fundy and Nova Scotia's Atlantic coast the strongest shore fisheries. Note: Gulf-side waters (NB Gulf shore, PEI, NS's Northumberland Strait) currently run zero retention on pollock — catch and release only there.

sections.heading: Know the Fish
sections.body_md:
Pollock (*Pollachius virens*), also called Boston bluefish, coalfish, or saithe, is a member of the cod family (Gadidae) but built and behaves differently from cod and haddock. Look for an olive-green to smoky brown or black back fading to silvery-grey sides and belly, a fairly straight pale lateral line, a forked tail (cod and haddock have squared/slightly rounded tails), and a slightly protruding lower jaw. The chin barbel that's obvious on cod is tiny or absent on pollock.

Juvenile pollock under about two years old move into shallow inshore water, hanging around wharves, breakwaters, kelp beds, and rocky intertidal structure. These young fish are commonly called "harbor pollock" by anglers and are usually the fish caught from shore in the 1-3 lb class. Adults move offshore onto banks and ledges, school more tightly in open water, and can reach 24-36 inches and 6-12+ lbs. Pollock are active, visual predators that chase baitfish, sandeels, and crustaceans well up in the water column, including right to the surface, which is why they're a favorite light-tackle target: unlike cod and haddock, you don't need to fish the bottom to find them.

sections.heading: When to Go
sections.body_md:
### Season
Pollock are catchable spring through fall wherever they're legal to retain (see Regulations). Nova Scotia's Bay of Fundy/Atlantic coast fishery is essentially open most of the year under DFO Maritimes rules (closed only in January), but summer and fall are when inshore "harbor pollock" show up thick around wharves and breakwaters.

### Time of Day
Dusk is repeatedly cited by NS anglers as the peak window: pollock push baitfish right to the surface in low light and feed aggressively near the top, making them visible and easy to target with light gear. Early morning can also produce, especially with surface activity from diving birds or breaking bait.

### Tide
A moving tide with current pushing past a wharf, breakwater, or point concentrates baitfish and pollock with it, following the same general pattern as mackerel in the same waters.

sections.heading: Where to Find Them
sections.body_md:
Pollock relate to structure and current the same way mackerel and striped bass do: wharves, breakwaters, rocky points, and ledges with moving water nearby.

**Bay of Fundy / Saint John area (NB):** St. Andrews holds summer inshore pollock fishable from piers and breakwaters, with small boats working rips and ledges on calmer tides. Around Saint John, Martins Wharf, Little Lepreaux, Beaver Harbour, and Blacks Harbour are named spots for pollock (and mackerel/flounder), and the shuttle dock below the restaurants at Reversing Falls West is specifically called out as good for pollock and striped bass.

**Nova Scotia:** The rocky Atlantic coastline, its wharves and breakwaters, gives easy shore access to pollock alongside mackerel and striped bass. The Bay of Fundy side of the province is noted as a strong winter/early-season haddock-and-pollock destination as well as a summer inshore fishery.

**PEI:** Pollock show up in PEI waters alongside mackerel, striped bass, and flounder, and any working wharf in summer is worth trying, though PEI's shore fishery leans more heavily toward mackerel — check with the local wharf authority before fishing from any working wharf.

As with any wharf fishing, get permission where required and stay clear of working boat traffic and gear.

sections.heading: Gear
sections.body_md:
| Item | Recommendation |
|---|---|
| Rod (spin) | Light-to-medium spinning rod, 7-9 ft, fast action tip for sensitivity — pollock hit hard and fight harder than their size suggests. |
| Line | 15-20 lb braid with a 15-20 lb fluorocarbon or mono leader; step up to 30 lb+ braid on heavier bottom gear for bigger offshore-caliber fish. |
| Jigs/lures | Mackerel jigs, flashy metal spoons/casting jigs (1/2-2 oz), white or chartreuse bucktails (6-12 oz for deeper boat work) with a soft-plastic swimbait trailer. |
| Bait (bottom rig) | Worms, cut herring, or smoked/oily herring strips — the oil trail draws fish in. |
| Fly | 8-9 weight rod with a fast-sinking line; sandeel or baitfish streamer patterns. |
| Extras | Pliers, a landing net or gaff for boat use, a cooler with ice. |

sections.heading: Technique: Jigging (Wharf, Breakwater, or Boat)
sections.body_md:
Pollock are visual, aggressive feeders and respond best to a lure worked with speed and flash rather than fished dead-still on bottom.

1. Cast a jig, spoon, or bucktail-with-swimbait-trailer out and let it sink — near the surface at dusk when fish are showing, or down toward structure/bottom if nothing's visible on top.
2. Use a sharp, snapping lift of the rod tip (about 12-18 inches) followed by dropping the tip and letting the lure flutter back down on slack line — this "snap-jigging" or "yo-yo" action imitates a fleeing baitfish and is the standard producer for pollock.
3. On hookup, keep steady pressure and don't horse the fish — pollock make hard, driving runs and will find any slack to throw the hook, especially near a wharf's pilings or rocks.
4. If fish are visibly busting bait on the surface (birds diving, boils), a straight fast, steady retrieve with a casting spoon works as well as jigging and covers water faster.
5. From a boat over structure, work a bucktail/swimbait jig vertically through the water column rather than pinning it to bottom — pollock often suspend well above the bottom over ledges and wrecks.

sections.heading: Technique: Bait Fishing from a Wharf
sections.body_md:
A simpler approach for harbor pollock around wharves and breakwaters:

1. Rig a simple bottom or float rig with worms, cut herring, or a small mackerel-strip bait.
2. Fish it near pilings, current seams, or drop-offs adjacent to the wharf structure where baitfish concentrate.
3. Smoked or oily herring is specifically noted by NB anglers as effective — the scent trail pulls fish in even when they're not actively feeding on top.
4. Expect mixed catches of pollock, mackerel, and flounder on the same bait rigs in these areas.

sources.label: newbrunswickfishing.com forum, Fishing for Pollock

sections.heading: Handling & Release
sections.body_md:
- Pollock fight hard and can be foul-hooked or deep-hooked when working fast jigs aggressively; use pliers to remove hooks quickly and minimize handling time on fish you plan to release.
- On the Gulf side of NB/PEI/NS, pollock currently must be released — handle with wet hands, avoid the gills, and get the fish back in the water quickly to maximize survival.
- Where retention is legal (NS Maritimes-region waters), bleed and ice fish promptly if keeping them for the table — pollock flesh holds up reasonably well but still benefits from quick icing like any groundfish.

sources.label: DFO — Recreational Groundfish Fishery, Southern Gulf of St. Lawrence

sections.heading: Conservation & Consumption Notes
sections.body_md:
Regulations differ sharply by DFO region for this species, and it matters a lot which side of the Maritimes you're fishing:

- **DFO Gulf Region** (NB Gulf shore, PEI, NS's Northumberland Strait/Gulf side): recreational groundfish rules for 2026 set **zero retention on pollock** — anglers may fish for them but must release everything caught, even during the open Cod/White Hake season window. Treat pollock here as catch-and-release only.
- **DFO Maritimes Region** (NS's Bay of Fundy and Atlantic coast, Halifax Harbour and west, and the Hartlen Point-to-Cape-North zone): pollock may be retained as part of the general daily groundfish bag limit (10 fish total in the Halifax-and-west/Bay of Fundy zone, 5 fish total in the Hartlen Point-east zone), with no pollock-specific bag or size limit found in the current notice — pollock simply counts toward the aggregate groundfish limit alongside species like haddock and flounder.

Given how different these rules are between the Gulf and Maritimes sides, and because DFO regularly issues updated variation orders, confirm current-year rules for your exact fishing location before keeping any pollock. Stock-wise, Gulf of Maine/Western Atlantic pollock are generally reported as not overfished with no overfishing occurring, and pollock is a low-mercury, popular sustainable-seafood choice on the table — mild, white, flaky flesh, slightly richer/darker than haddock due to higher fat content, good baked, broiled, fried, or smoked.
